# ipole_abc dataset v2: movie viewer

Pick a movie with the slider (or type its id) to see its parameters and all its frames, stacked per frame:
**A** = disk + spot (top row), **B** = disk only (middle; one image per movie, repeated under every frame), **C** = spot only (bottom).

* Frame titles: time in minutes; a **red** title marks the frames of the n=0 window (the spot's direct image, one orbit).
  The per-frame fluxes (Jy) are printed in each panel.
* **scale**: *shared* uses one colour scale for all three rows (brightness comparable across A, B, C); *per row* gives each row its own.
  *log* shows 3 decades below the maximum.
* **refresh list** picks up movies written since the notebook started (the worker array is still running).
* Typing the id of a manifest row that was rendered but dropped shows its failure reason.
* Images: 128 x 128 px over 32 M (1 M = 5.19 uas), shown as `imshow(img.T, origin='lower')`, x to the right, y up.

# ML results on the v2 dataset

The two machine-learning tasks of `ipole_abc_ml` (results notebook `/scratch/ralbe/ipole_abc_ml/abc_unet_results.ipynb`) re-trained on
the 10 000 `in_10k` movies of this dataset, code and runs in `/scratch/ralbe/ipole_abc_ml_v2` (README there).

* **Part 1 — task 1 (image → image).** From the movie A (disk + spot), predict the image of the spot alone, C, frame by frame.
  Five network designs, each with input I and input IQU.
* **Part 2 — task 2 (movie → numbers).** From the same movie, predict inclination, spin, θ_spot, the orbit radius r_spot and the
  period P (v1 Parts 2 and 4 in one: the v2 networks always predict all five).
* **Part 3 — task 1 on blurred movies.** The task-1 networks re-trained on movies blurred to EHT / ngEHT resolution (no noise).

Section numbers follow the v1 notebook. Runs still training show up as empty rows / cells marked with their status; re-running the
cells fills them in (the notebook updates its own caches of pixel errors and centroid angles).
Sliders and check boxes need a live kernel; a static run (`NB_HEADLESS=1`) shows one default movie instead.
6:
## 0. Data, normalisation and error measures

**Frames.** From every movie only the window from the first frame with any spot light (`spot_first`) to the last one with any of it
(`spot_last`) is used: **T** = 10 – 19 frames, 127 519 frames in all. Within the window, frames with the spot's direct image are
**n = 0 frames**; the late frames that contain only light that looped around the hole are **n ≥ 1 only** frames (the hardest ones).

**Normalisation.** Each movie is divided by one number **s** (`scale`, Jy/pixel) = the brightest pixel of A (Stokes I) in its window.
Networks see and predict these movie-normalised images; multiplying back by s gives Jy/pixel, which is how the physical errors below
are computed. (v2 movies have ⟨F_A⟩ = 1.5 – 3 Jy, so a Jy error has the same meaning for every movie, unlike v1.)

**Split.** By movie: train 7 998, val 1 001, test 1 001 (stratified as in v1). Every number here is on the **1 001 test movies
(12 655 frames)**.

**Brightness.** v2 is conditioned on the spot share ⟨F_C⟩/⟨F_A⟩ ∈ [0.01, 0.5] (`share`), not on log R; log R = log₁₀(⟨F_C⟩/F_B)
then runs from about −2 to 0 (the spot is never brighter than the disk on average).

| name | definition | read it as |
|---|---|---|
| **relL2** | ‖Ĉ − C‖ / ‖C‖ per frame (‖X‖ = √Σ pixels X²) | 0 = perfect, 1 = as bad as predicting nothing |
| **flux error** | \|ln(F̂ / F)\|, F = Σ pixels of C | 0.01 ≈ total spot flux off by 1 % |
| **MAE [µJy/px]** | mean over all 128 × 128 pixels and over the test frames of \|Ĉ − C\| · s | the physical error per pixel (1 px = 0.25 M = 1.30 µas); × 16 384 = summed \|error\| per frame |
| **empty** | the same for Ĉ = 0: mean \|C\| · s | the error of not predicting any spot; **MAE / empty** = share of it that is left |
| **ΔF [mJy]** | (F̂ − F) · s per frame | error of the total spot flux in mJy |
| **median, p90** | over test frames | typical frame / one of the worst 10 % |
| **PA₀, PA₁, DPA** | position angles of the n = 0 and n ≥ 1 centroids and their difference (Section 1.9) | degrees |

# Part 1 — Task 1: predict the spot image C from the movie A (unblurred)

### The five methods
All five are **U-Nets** (an encoder that shrinks the image step by step, a decoder that grows it back, with skip connections between
matching sizes). They differ in how much of the movie they see when predicting frame t:

| method | what it sees to predict frame t | idea |
|---|---|---|
| **1 single frame** | only frame t of A, rescaled so its brightest pixel is 1 | baseline: recognise the spot from one picture |
| **2 frame + neighbours** | frames t−2 … t+2 of A (mirrored at the window ends), plus the movie's per-pixel **median** and **minimum** of A_I | the disk is static and the spot moves, so median / minimum ≈ the disk |
| **3 whole movie (3D)** | all frames at once as one block (time × height × width), 3D U-Net without pooling in time, plus a temporal-mean path | can follow the spot through time |
| **4 disk subtraction** | all frames; an encoder pooled over time estimates the disk B̂, then Ĉ_t = A_t,I − B̂ + a learned correction (zero-initialised U-Net) | uses A ≈ B + C; the correction is needed because the disk also absorbs part of the spot's light. Training adds L1 on B̂ against the true B |
| **5 disk subtraction + neighbours** | as 4, but the correction U-Net is as large as method 2's and sees frames t−2 … t+2 of both A and A − B̂ | the combination of 4 (best typical frame in v1) and 2 (fewest bad failures in v1) |

**Input I / IQU.** Each method is trained with Stokes I only and with I, Q, U; the output is always Stokes I of the spot (n = 0 + n ≥ 1).

**Training** (same as v1). Images pass through a soft logarithm z = asinh(x / 10⁻³) / asinh(10³) so faint n ≥ 1 light (~1 % of the peak)
still counts; loss = L1 in z. AdamW, lr 10⁻³, weight decay 10⁻⁴, warm-up + cosine decay; 25 epochs (methods 1–2, batches of 32 frames)
or 60 epochs (methods 3–5, batches of 4 movies); bf16 on Ampere / Ada GPUs; the epoch with the best validation loss is kept.

### 1.9 Where is the spot? Centroids and position angles of the n = 0 and n ≥ 1 images

**Truth.** v2 stores, for every frame, the exact direct image `Cn0` (C − Cn0 is the n ≥ 1 part), whether each part is present
(`n0_present`, `n1_present`: flux > 1 % of its peak over the movie) and its flux-weighted centroid (`cen_n0`, `cen_n1`, from the 256 px
render, negative pixels dropped). So the true PA₀, PA₁ and DPA need no guessing; they are labelled **exact** below.

**Predictions.** A network predicts only the total Ĉ. To read PA₀ and PA₁ off it, Ĉ is split with the v1 rule
(`code/dpa.py`): pixels above 0.3 % of the frame's brightest pixel are grouped into connected blobs; the blob farthest from the black
hole's critical curve (flux-weighted mean distance d̄ > 0.3 M, > 30 px, > 2 % of the brightest blob's flux; the curve is computed from the
movie's true spin and inclination, thin cyan line) is n = 0, all other blobs are n ≥ 1. The same rule applied to the **true** C
(**segmented true C**, grey) shows how much of the error is the rule itself: it is the floor for the networks.
(On v2 it puts 96 % of the flux in the right class on 40 test movies; 99 % on v1. v2 spots orbit at 3 – 7 M, closer to the photon ring.)

**Angles.** Centroid (x̄, ȳ) = brightness-weighted mean position, black hole at (0, 0); **PA** = atan2(−x̄, ȳ), degrees counter-clockwise
from "up"; **DPA = PA₁ − PA₀** wrapped to −180° … 180°; R̄ = distance of the centroid from the hole. When the n ≥ 1 light is a nearly
complete ring its centroid is near the centre and its PA is meaningless: frames with true R̄₁ < 2 M are drawn open and left out of the statistics.

Pick a test movie (same slider as 1.6), a network (unblurred runs) and the frames. Top: the movie segmented three ways (exact split,
rule on true C, rule on the prediction; cyan contour / × = n = 0, green / + = n ≥ 1). Bottom: PA₀(t), PA₁(t), DPA(t).

### 1.10 Recovering PA₀, PA₁ and the DPA over all 1 001 test movies
For every test frame where the exact truth **and** the segmented prediction both contain a part: \|ΔPA\| = \|wrap(PA_pred − PA_exact)\|
(median, 90th percentile). `missed %` = share of the frames that have the part in the truth where the prediction has none;
`invented %` = share of the frames without it where the prediction shows one. n ≥ 1 frames with true R̄₁ < 2 M are left out (PA undefined).
**DPA** columns: \|wrap(DPA_pred − DPA_exact)\| over frames where both have both parts. The first row applies the rule to the true C: the floor.
Most "invented" n ≥ 1 parts are a matter of thresholds, as the floor row shows: the dataset counts a part as present above 1 % of its peak
over the movie, the rule keeps any blob above 0.3 % of the frame's brightest pixel, so faint late n ≥ 1 light counts only for the rule.

# Part 2 — Task 2: inclination, spin, θ_spot, r_spot and period from the movie

(v1 Parts 2 and 4 together: in v2 every task-2 network predicts the five numbers.)

**Input:** the same frames A as task 1 (same movies and split), the time of every frame, and three numbers an observer would know: the
movie's brightness s, the cadence and the number of frames T. **Output:** per movie, **inc**, **a**, **θ_spot**, **r_spot** and
**log₁₀ P** (P = orbital period in minutes), each with an uncertainty σ (Gaussian likelihood).

**Networks.** A CNN turns each frame into 256 features (the same CNN for every frame), the frame time is added, then
**pool** averages the frame features (learned weights, mean, max) into a small head, or **xattn** lets the frame features attend to each
other in a 4-layer transformer with a summary token. Each with input I and IQU, on the three data versions (12 settings).
Targets are scaled for the v2 prior: (cos i + 0.75)/0.25, a/0.99, (θ_spot − 90)/30, (r_spot − 5)/2, (log P − 1.75)/0.5;
loss MSE + Gaussian NLL; 0–2 random frames dropped in training; 100 epochs, AdamW 3·10⁻⁴, wd 0.05.

**Joint or separate networks.** Before the grid, pool / I / unblurred was trained 4× as one 5-output network and 4× as five 1-output
networks; `decide.py` picks the design for all 12 settings (separate only if significantly better for ≥ 1 target, Bonferroni).
The cells below use whichever design was run. Caveats: in v2 r_spot is independent of the ISCO (the v1 spin ↔ r_spot shortcut is gone);
the period is still nearly fixed by the frame times (P = cadence × n_on), so log P is easy.

# Part 3 — Task 1 on blurred movies (telescope-like observations)

The same five methods, re-trained on blurred copies of the same movies (same split and frames). No noise is added.

### How the movies were blurred
* **Beam.** Every Stokes plane of A, B **and** C is convolved with a round Gaussian (0.25 M per pixel):

  | beam | FWHM | σ | meaning |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | **ngEHT** (`ngeht_n0`) | 8/3 M ≈ 14 µas | 4.53 px | a planned, sharper next-generation EHT |
  | **EHT** (`eht_n0`) | 4 M ≈ 21 µas | 6.79 px | about today's EHT at 230 GHz |

  The photon ring is ~10 M across, so under the EHT beam the thin n ≥ 1 arcs are smeared into the direct image.
* **Normalisation.** Each blurred movie is divided by its own brightest blurred pixel (new `scale`; the networks' inputs again peak at 1).
* **Target.** The networks see blurred A and predict **blurred** C (what the spot alone would look like through the same telescope; no
  sharpening). Scores are against the blurred C, so relL2 is not directly comparable with Part 1 (a smooth image is easier to match pixel by
  pixel). The physical error per pixel is in Jy/pixel of the blurred images; the total flux is unchanged by the blur, so ΔF in mJy
  compares directly across versions.

Run `opt5_I_eht_n0` = method 5, input I, EHT-blurred movies. Unlike v1, every method × input is planned on both beams.

63:
### 3.7 Reading of the results
*(updated 2026-10-19; all 30 task-1 runs finished: 5 methods × I / IQU × unblurred / ngEHT / EHT, one seed each)*
* **Blur makes the scores better, not worse.** Against the blurred truth, the best median relL2 is 0.020 (method 5, ngEHT) vs 0.039 for
  the best on sharp movies (method 2, input I); 75 – 81 % of frames are below relL2 0.05 for methods 2 and 5 (sharp: 64 % at best).
  The blurred target is smoother and so easier to match pixel by pixel; the networks still separate spot from disk.
* **In Jy it holds up too.** With input I the error per pixel drops by 20 – 33 % with either beam for methods 2 – 5, but rises for
  method 1 (+19 – 21 %).
  The like-for-like number, the total spot flux, is as good as on sharp movies: median \|ΔF\| 2.7 – 2.9 mJy (method 2 / 5, input I, ngEHT)
  vs 3.1 – 3.4 mJy for the best sharp runs, i.e. < 1 % of the mean spot flux (423 mJy). Method 1 is the exception (3.1 → 5.0 mJy).
* **Methods 2 and 5 lead; on the hard frames method 2 is ahead** (as in v1). Median relL2 under blur (input I, ngEHT / EHT): method 5
  0.020 / 0.023, method 2 0.022 / 0.024, method 4 0.028 / 0.031, method 3 0.031 / 0.030, method 1 0.039 / 0.037. On frames with only
  n ≥ 1 light: method 2 0.060 / 0.063, method 5 0.064 / 0.085, method 4 0.104 / 0.118; p90: 0.089 / 0.096, 0.092 / 0.114, 0.147 / 0.158.
  Plain disk subtraction (method 4) stays weakest on the tail, as on sharp movies (p90 0.24): a fixed disk estimate B̂ does not help
  with the faint late light, looking at the neighbouring frames does.
* **ngEHT vs EHT**: the sharper beam is slightly better for methods 2, 4 and 5 (method 5: \|ΔF\| 2.9 vs 3.5 mJy, only-n ≥ 1 relL2 0.064 vs
  0.085); for methods 1 and 3 the two beams tie. These scores are against the correspondingly blurred truth, so they do not show the lost
  detail itself.
* **Polarisation (IQU) gives no consistent gain.** Under blur the differences are small (\|ΔMAE\| ≤ 0.1 µJy/px, 3.4): IQU helps a little
  for method 3 and method 5 on EHT (−0.09 / −0.06 µJy/px) and method 4 on ngEHT (−0.06), and hurts method 2 on ngEHT (+0.10). On sharp
  movies IQU helps methods 3 and 4 slightly, but methods 1 and 5 with IQU are clearly worse (median relL2 0.068 / 0.063 vs 0.042). Both
  of those runs converged to a higher plateau (method 1 IQU started with an all-zero output), and the gap disappears on both blurred
  versions, so it is most likely a training outcome of this single seed rather than polarisation hurting; a second seed would settle it.
